Australia's Izzi Batt-Doyle took more than two minutes off her personal best, finishing sixth in the women's race at the Chicago Marathon. (Supplied: Jan Figueroa)

Adelaide runner Izzi Batt-Doyle lowered her own personal best by more than two minutes, breaking the Australian women's marathon record in Chicago.

Her time of 2:20:38 took 46 seconds off the existing record, held by Jess Stenson.

Batt-Doyle, who was paced by her fiancé Riley Cocks, finished sixth in the women's race at the Chicago Marathon behind winner Hawi Feysa of Ethiopia.

Adelaide's Izzi Batt-Doyle is Australia's new marathon queen after breaking the national record with a stunning run at the year's penultimate major, the Chicago Marathon.

Batt-Doyle ran a time of 2:20:38 to take 46 seconds off the mark set by fellow South Australian Jess Stenson in Valencia in December.

It also lowered the 31-year-old's own personal best by two minutes and 21 seconds.

"I'm very, very happy. I feel a sense of relief, because it's something I really felt I could achieve and it's been on my mind the past couple of years," Batt-Doyle said.

"I'm really proud I could achieve it today and I'm so happy."

Tigst Assefa ran the final two kilometres of the Berlin Marathon with a badly damaged Achilles tendon, which required immediate surgery to repair. She still ran the third-fastest women's marathon in history.

Batt-Doyle was sixth overall in the women's race, which was won by defending champion Hawi Feysa of Ethiopia in 2:13:33.

"The field here is so great, but smaller on the professional side," Batt-Doyle said.

"You don't have masses of people in groups."

Batt-Doyle was paced by her fiancé Riley Cocks.

"[We were] isolated the whole race," she said.

"The gun went off and second kilometre it was just the two of us, because we were running between groups.

"I spent most of the race trusting our plan and the pacing strategy we had hoped to run the first half in, and hope that I would feel strong in the second half."

Batt-Doyle's race was a model of control, with her splits barely moving. Every 5km block landed between 16:36 and 16:47, holding her at about 3:19 to 3:21 per kilometre from the opening kilometres to the final stretch.

Marathon legend Eliud Kipchoge has time to slow down and wave at the crowds at the MCG and still break the race record at the Melbourne Marathon.

She went through halfway in 1:10:29 and then ran the second half in about 1:10:09, giving her a 20-second negative split.

"We went through halfway in under the time needed to run 2:21, but I wasn't sure because I felt like I was slowing in the second half as it was warmer, and just the general fatigue of the marathon," Batt-Doyle said.

"It was quite warm and we knew going into this week that it was going to be a bit warmer than ideal marathon conditions, but we did what we could do to prepare for that.

"That's hydrating a lot beforehand, and every opportunity that there were water cups I was splashing three or four water cups to keep cool."

But Batt-Doyle didn't fade in the conditions, with her quickest 5km split of 16:36 coming between 35km and 40km. She covered the last 2.2km at about 3:14 per kilometre, when she started to sense the record was hers.

"There is a small hill about 400 to go, and then you turn into the last 150 metres, and I saw the clock and that's when I really started celebrating," she said.

"It was quite emotional. You can think you can do it and hope you can do it, and be on pace to do it, but there is so much that can happen in the last 5 kilometres, or last 1 kilometre or even the last 400 metres.

Batt-Doyle said she was proud to join the list of previous Australian record-holders that included Stenson, Sinead Diver and Benita Willis.

"I think it's really validating for the hard work I've put in and it feels really special to be part of history, because there have been some fantastic runners before me, and fantastic runners to come," she said.

"I really feel honoured, that sums it up. To be in that class of athletes. I'm really proud of that."

Kenya's Amos Kipruto won the men's race in 2:01:09.
